question: What is the meaning of the product is designed for recycling to maintain material quality in relation to recycling?
data_point: the product is designed for recycling to maintain material quality
description: The phrase "product is designed for recycling to maintain material quality" implies that the product has been specifically engineered with recycling in mind, ensuring that the materials used in the product can be effectively recycled without compromising their quality. This design approach facilitates the recycling process, allowing for the recovery of high-quality materials, which is crucial for maintaining the sustainability and efficiency of recycling operations. This concept is closely related to the idea of designing for disassembly and circularity, where products are created with the end-of-life phase in mind, enabling easier recycling and material recovery.

To support the decision to select components for a second life, man-
ufacturers see value in using a digital product passport to access data
about environmental life cycle impacts (e.g., carbon footprint) on both
a product level and a component level. Combined with the ﬁnancial
value of a given component (e.g., through a bill of materials), this
would enable manufacturers to target the components with the highest
environmental and ﬁnancial impact. Closely tied to this scoping process,
remanufacturing activities – particularly in the case of long-life products
– are also challenged by frequent design changes with little attention to
the cross-model compatibility of components. Already now, but more
so in upcoming product generations where circular principles are likely
to become integrated into design, practitioners recommend that a digi-
tal product passport should contain information about the compatibility
of components. This would add ﬂexibility to the value retention options
and partially remedy the challenges of foraging for post-market mate-
rials, as imposed by low product return rates. Finally, in cases where
components or materials must be sent to suppliers or third-party
recycling companies, respectively, a digital product passport is consid-
ered suitable for providing information about the actors involved in
the production and circulation of a given product, thereby identifying
subsequent trajectories in a cascaded ﬂow of products.

4.4. Supplier: remanufacture of components
Similar to product manufacturers, supplier engagement in closing
resource loops is conditioned by reverse product and material ﬂows,
which provide new sourcing opportunities. Either components may be
returned as an extension of the manufacturer's take-back programmes,
or they are harvested from scrap vendors. In both cases, better access to
high-quality data about a component (as facilitated by a digital product
passport) is considered a key enabler for higher degrees of value
utilisation. For example, rather than remelting – and thus recycling –
aluminium and steel components, certain types of data may create fruit-
ful conditions for exploring remanufacturing options. As exempliﬁed by
interviewees, such data could concern material composition, as well as a
list of hazardous substances. Even in closed loops where any given sup-
plier receives its own components, detailed insight into material com-
position is needed due to frequently occurring design changes and
chemical thresholds, as induced by changing regulation. Related to
this, suppliers consider a digital product passport a coveted platform
for accessing data about recycled content. Although it is not considered
essential, this could support suppliers in securing the quality and dura-
bility of remanufactured components, as well as tracking such content
throughout multiple life cycles.
This is summarised in Fig. 5. While material composition and a list of

3.3. Benefits of DPPs for recycle strategies
DPPs enhance recycling efficiency by tracking product material 
composition and recyclability. By providing access to data regarding 
what materials are used and their potential for recyclability, DPPs 
enable recyclers to identify and segregate materials more accurately and 
efficiently, thereby improving the overall efficiency of recycling oper­
ations (Adisorn et al., 2021). This targeted approach minimizes waste 
and maximizes the recovery of valuable materials (Berg et al., 2022). 
Furthermore, DPPs can support the implementation of intelligent waste 
management systems. These systems leverage the detailed product data 
contained within DPPs to optimize waste materials’ sorting, processing, 
and recycling (Chauhan, A. et al., 2021; Chauhan, C. et al., 2022). By 
integrating DPP data with smart waste management technologies, 
stakeholders can streamline recycling workflows, reduce operational 
costs, and enhance the quality of recycled outputs (Gligoric et al., 2019). 
DPPs provide product information, including material compositions, 
dismantling procedures, and end-of-life handling protocols. This infor­
mation is central for recyclers and waste management professionals, as it 
informs the best practices for dismantling and processing products at the 
end of their lives (Ducuing and Reich, 2023). By understanding the 
specific requirements for handling each product, recyclers can minimize 
environmental impacts and increase the efficiency of recycling processes 
(Kristoffersen et al., 2020). The improvement of recycling processes 
through DPPs is a significant advancement. By ensuring that all stake­
holders have access to detailed and accurate product information, DPPs 
facilitate better decision-making and operational practices (Gong et al., 
2022). This leads to more effective recycling methodologies, higher 
material recovery rates, and reduced contamination of recyclable 
streams (Khan, S. A. R. et al., 2021).
3.3.1. Data needs for recycle strategies
Advancing the recycling strategy within the CE necessitates under­
standing several critical data points, each contributing to optimizing 
recycling processes. This integration of knowledge ensures the sustain­
ability of recycling operations and enhances their efficiency, thereby 
promoting a more effective CE. The foundation of effective recycling lies 
in the detailed knowledge of material composition. Understanding the 
exact materials of a product allows for the appropriate recycling 
methods to be applied, ensuring materials are recovered efficiently and 
sustainably (Bisinella et al., 2017). Coupled with this, the recyclability 
of materials plays an important role in determining the life cycle po­
tential of materials used in products. Identifying highly recyclable ma­
terials promotes their selection in design processes and guarantees that 
end-of-life products are directed toward suitable recycling pathways, 
minimizing waste (Kanwal et al., 2021). Navigating the complex land­
scape of local and global recycling regulations is necessary for main­
taining compliance and optimizing recycling rates. These regulations 
dictate the proper handling, transportation, and processing of re­
cyclables, underscoring the importance of regulatory knowledge in 
facilitating global recycling efforts (Salmenper¨a, 2021).
Moreover, product return guidelines are essential for reintegrating 
products into recycling. Companies can enhance product recycling rates 
by outlining consumer return processes and fostering greater consumer 
participation in CE strategies (Malmgren and M¨otsch Larsson, 2020). 
Disassembly instructions are essential for efficiently dismantling prod­
ucts, a step critical for recovering valuable materials.
